rover-lunar-lrv.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV)
rover-lunar-lrv.story: Imagine a car that travels folded up like a beach chair inside a spacecraft. That is how the Lunar Rover arrived: folded against the side of the landing module. The astronauts pulled on some straps and the car unfolded by itself. With it, the crews of Apollo 15, 16 and 17 could drive kilometers away from the landing site to look for ancient rocks. At the end of each mission, the rover stayed parked on the Moon. There was no room to bring it back, so today three electric cars sit on the lunar surface.
rover-lunar-lrv.science: The rover ran on silver-zinc batteries that could not be recharged, and each wheel had its own electric motor. Its tires were not made of rubber: they were a mesh of steel wire with titanium plates, because rubber would have been damaged by the extreme cold and heat. Thanks to the distances they covered, the astronauts collected samples from different terrains, including Apollo 15's famous “Genesis Rock”, a piece of the Moon's oldest crust.
rover-lunar-lrv.today: The three rovers are still where they were left, without power. NASA's LRO probe has photographed them from orbit, and its images still show their wheel tracks, because on the Moon there is no wind or rain to erase them.
rover-lunar-lrv.fun: On Apollo 17 a fender broke. The astronauts fixed it with duct tape and laminated maps. And the rover's camera, controlled from Houston, filmed the liftoff of the spacecraft heading home: nobody was there to record it!
sourceTitles: LROC: images of the Apollo sites

retrorreflectores-apollo.name: Laser retroreflectors
retrorreflectores-apollo.place: Sea of Tranquility, Fra Mauro and Hadley
retrorreflectores-apollo.story: Of everything the astronauts left on the Moon, one object still works every single day, and it does not even need electricity. It is a panel full of small glass prisms called a retroreflector. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin set up the first one in 1969. Later, Apollo 14 and Apollo 15 left two more. Ever since, observatories on Earth have been firing laser beams at them and waiting for the light to bounce back.
retrorreflectores-apollo.science: A corner prism sends light back exactly the way it came. By measuring how long the laser takes to go and come back (about 2.5 seconds), we know the distance to the Moon with millimeter precision. That is how we found out the Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 centimeters every year. These measurements are also used to test Einstein's theory of relativity.
retrorreflectores-apollo.today: It is one of the few Apollo experiments still active. Of the trillions of photons that are sent, only a handful come back, so scientists need large telescopes and very sensitive detectors.
retrorreflectores-apollo.fun: Retroreflectors work like the reflectors on a bicycle or the reflective strips on a safety vest. The same idea, but 384,000 kilometers away!
sourceTitles: APOLLO: Apache Point Lunar Laser Ranging

eagle-etapa-descenso.name: Eagle descent stage
eagle-etapa-descenso.story: The Eagle lunar module had two parts. The top part carried the astronauts; the bottom part, with its golden legs, was the landing engine. When Armstrong and Aldrin finished their moonwalk, the top part lifted off using the bottom part as a launch pad. The descent stage stayed forever in the Sea of Tranquility, surrounded by footprints, bags, boots and tools that were no longer needed.
eagle-etapa-descenso.science: Its engine was one of the first rockets that could speed up and slow down like a car's pedal, something essential for touching down gently. During the descent, Armstrong had to fly by hand to avoid a field of boulders, and he landed with less than a minute of reserve fuel. That experience helped design the landings of the missions that followed.
eagle-etapa-descenso.today: It is still in place, next to five other Apollo descent stages. The LRO probe has photographed the site: you can make out the spacecraft and the paths the astronauts left as they walked.
eagle-etapa-descenso.fun: One of its legs carries a plaque that reads: “Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind.”
sourceTitles: NASA History: Catalogue of man-made material on the Moon (PDF)

alsep-sismometros.name: ALSEP science stations
alsep-sismometros.story: The astronauts could only stay on the Moon for a few days, but they wanted to keep listening to it after they left. So they left behind small automatic laboratories called ALSEP. Each one had seismometers, heat probes, solar wind detectors and an antenna to send data to Earth. For almost eight years these stations sent information nonstop, until NASA switched them off in 1977.
alsep-sismometros.science: The seismometers discovered that the Moon has “moonquakes”. To study its interior, NASA deliberately crashed rocket parts into the surface. After one of those impacts, the Moon rang like a bell for about an hour. Those vibrations revealed that the Moon has layers: a crust, a mantle and a core. Power came from a generator that turned the heat of plutonium into electricity.
alsep-sismometros.today: The stations are still on the Moon, switched off. Their data, however, are still being studied: today's scientists analyze them with modern computers and find new moonquakes that went unnoticed before.
alsep-sismometros.fun: Apollo 11 carried a simpler version called EASEP. Its seismometer even picked up the footsteps of Armstrong and Aldrin walking nearby.
sourceTitles: LPI: Apollo missions and their experiments

surveyor-3.name: Surveyor 3
surveyor-3.story: Before sending people, NASA needed to know whether the lunar ground could hold the weight of a spacecraft. So it sent the Surveyor robots. Surveyor 3 had a bumpy landing: its engines did not shut off in time and it bounced three times before coming to rest. Even so, it worked, took thousands of photos and dug trenches with its arm. Two and a half years later it got an unexpected visit: the Apollo 12 astronauts landed about 180 meters away.
surveyor-3.science: Its mechanical scoop showed that the surface was firm, like packed wet sand, and that a crewed spacecraft would not sink. When Pete Conrad and Alan Bean visited Surveyor 3, they cut off its camera and other parts to bring them back to Earth. That let scientists study how the lunar environment affects materials after years of exposure.
surveyor-3.today: Most of the spacecraft is still in the Ocean of Storms. Its camera is at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington.
surveyor-3.fun: For years people said that some Earth bacteria had survived inside the camera. Today it is thought that it got contaminated when it was opened on Earth: a good lesson in why science always double-checks its results.

lcross.name: LCROSS
lcross.mission: Lunar Crater Observation and Sensing Satellite
lcross.story: Some spacecraft end their mission by crashing... on purpose. LCROSS traveled to the Moon together with the upper stage of its rocket, called Centaur. Near the south pole, the two separated. First, Centaur slammed into the dark floor of Cabeus Crater and kicked up a huge cloud of dust. LCROSS flew through that cloud, measuring everything it could, and four minutes later it crashed too.
lcross.science: The floor of some polar craters never gets sunlight and is one of the coldest places in the solar system. Scientists suspected there could be hidden ice there. LCROSS's instruments detected water in the cloud of material thrown up. It was key evidence that the Moon keeps ice at its poles.
lcross.today: The remains of LCROSS and Centaur lie in Cabeus Crater. Their discovery now guides plans to explore the lunar south pole, where water could be used for drinking or for making fuel.
lcross.fun: Lots of people gathered with telescopes to watch the crash, expecting a big flash... which could not be seen from Earth. What mattered was in the data, not in the show.

lro.name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
lro.story: This spacecraft is not abandoned: it is the caretaker of everything others left behind. LRO reached the Moon in 2009 and has been circling it ever since, taking pictures and measuring its surface. Thanks to it we can see, from Earth, the Apollo modules, the parked rovers and even the trails left by the astronauts' boots.
lro.science: LRO built the most detailed maps of the Moon that exist. Its camera can make out objects the size of a table, and other instruments measure the temperature of the ground and look for ice in craters. These maps are used to choose safe places for future crewed missions.
lro.today: It is still active after more than 17 years, far longer than planned. It is like a living archive: every new photo helps us see how the surface changes and find new craters made by meteorites.
lro.fun: LRO photographed the places where other spacecraft crashed, like the twin GRAIL probes, and so confirmed the exact spot of their impacts.

viking-1.name: Viking 1
viking-1.story: On July 20, 1976, exactly seven years after the first Moon landing, Viking 1 touched down on Mars. It was the first American spacecraft to work successfully on the Martian surface. It sent back photos of a red landscape full of rocks under a butterscotch sky. For more than six years it measured the Martian weather day after day, until a mistake in a command sent from Earth cut off communication in 1982.
viking-1.science: Viking carried a small laboratory to search for life: it scooped soil with an arm, mixed it with nutrients and watched whether “something” breathed or ate. The results were confusing and most scientists concluded there was no life, but there was a very strange soil chemistry. Those questions guided every Mars mission that came after.
viking-1.today: The spacecraft is still in Chryse Planitia, silent. It was renamed the “Thomas Mutch Memorial Station”, in honor of the leader of its imaging team.
viking-1.fun: Its twin, Viking 2, landed in another region and photographed frost covering the Martian ground in winter.

sojourner-pathfinder.name: Sojourner and Pathfinder
sojourner-pathfinder.story: Pathfinder arrived on Mars in a very fun way: wrapped in giant airbags, it bounced across the ground like a ball before stopping. When it opened, it let out Sojourner, a rover the size of a microwave oven. It was the first wheeled vehicle to roam another planet. It was meant to work for a week and lasted almost three months, studying rocks that the team named after cartoon characters.
sojourner-pathfinder.science: Sojourner had an instrument that analyzed what rocks were made of. It found rounded rocks and pebbles like the ones rivers leave behind, signs that water once flowed through that region. The mission also proved that landing could be done cheaply with airbags, an idea later used by Spirit and Opportunity.
sojourner-pathfinder.today: The Pathfinder lander, named the “Carl Sagan Memorial Station”, and little Sojourner are still in Ares Vallis, just a few meters apart.
sojourner-pathfinder.fun: The name Sojourner was suggested by a 12-year-old girl, Valerie Ambroise, in a school contest. She chose it in honor of Sojourner Truth, a civil rights champion.

spirit.name: Spirit
spirit.story: Spirit came to Mars for a three-month mission and kept working for more than six years. In 2006 one of its wheels jammed, so the team decided to drive it backwards, dragging the broken wheel. In 2009 it got stuck in soft sand at a place called Troy. Engineers tried to free it for months, but Martian winter arrived and Spirit stopped responding in March 2010.
spirit.science: Its broken wheel turned out to be a big help: by dragging it, Spirit scraped the ground and uncovered a white material made of almost pure silica. On Earth, that material forms in hot springs or volcanic steam vents, places microbes love to live. So an accident became one of its greatest discoveries.
spirit.today: Spirit is still stuck at Troy, covered in dust. Its mission was declared over in May 2011.
spirit.fun: Spirit and its twin Opportunity were launched a month apart and landed on opposite sides of Mars.

opportunity.name: Opportunity
opportunity.story: Opportunity, “Oppy” to its friends, had a lucky landing: it bounced and ended up right inside a small crater, like a hole in one in golf. It was meant to work for 90 days and stayed active for more than 14 years, driving farther than a marathon. In June 2018 a dust storm covered the whole planet, blocked the sunlight, and its solar panels stopped charging.
opportunity.science: Opportunity found small spheres of a mineral called hematite, which the team nicknamed “blueberries”. On Earth, these spheres usually form in water. Together with other layered rocks, they were proof that Meridiani once had liquid water, perhaps salty and acidic.
opportunity.today: It rests in Perseverance Valley, on the rim of Endeavour Crater. NASA sent more than a thousand calls before declaring the mission over in February 2019.
opportunity.fun: The phrase “My battery is low and it's getting dark” became famous. It was not a literal message: it was a poetic translation of its last data by a journalist.

phoenix.name: Phoenix
phoenix.story: Phoenix went somewhere nobody had visited: the icy plains near the north pole of Mars. With its robotic arm it dug trenches in the ground and found bright white bits. A few days later those bits had disappeared. What happened? They were water ice that turned into vapor once exposed to the Sun. When Martian winter came, Phoenix ran out of light and stopped communicating.
phoenix.science: Phoenix confirmed that there is water ice beneath the soil of the Martian arctic. It also discovered perchlorate, a salt that can lower the temperature at which water freezes, and it watched snow falling from the clouds, although the snow evaporated before reaching the ground.
phoenix.today: Photos taken years later from orbit showed that its solar panels broke under the weight of the carbon dioxide ice that piled up on top during the winter.
phoenix.fun: Phoenix is a library on Mars! It carries a DVD called “Visions of Mars”, with novels, stories and art about the red planet, plus thousands of people's names, meant for future explorers.

insight.name: InSight
insight.story: InSight did not come to look at the scenery: it came to listen to the heart of Mars. It set up a seismometer so sensitive it could feel vibrations smaller than the width of an atom. Over four years it recorded more than a thousand “marsquakes”. But Martian dust slowly covered its solar panels, until it stopped responding in December 2022.
insight.science: Marsquake waves travel through the planet and change depending on what they pass through, just like an ultrasound scan. With them, scientists measured the thickness of Mars's crust and found that its core is liquid and bigger than expected. InSight also had a drill, “the mole”, which could not bury itself because the soil kept clumping.
insight.today: InSight is still in Elysium Planitia, covered in dust. Its data are still used to understand how rocky planets form, including Earth.
insight.fun: InSight also detected meteorite impacts. Afterwards, orbiting spacecraft photographed the freshly formed craters, and some of them had uncovered ice!

ingenuity.name: Ingenuity
ingenuity.story: Ingenuity traveled to Mars tucked under the Perseverance rover. It was an experiment: nobody knew whether a helicopter could fly in such thin air. On April 19, 2021 it rose about 3 meters for 39 seconds and became the first machine to make a powered flight on another planet. It was meant to fly five times. It flew 72. In January 2024 its blades were damaged and it could no longer take off.
ingenuity.science: The air on Mars is barely 1% as dense as Earth's air. To get lift, Ingenuity's blades spun at about 2,400 revolutions per minute, much faster than an ordinary helicopter. Its success showed that future missions can use aircraft to explore places a rover cannot reach.
ingenuity.today: It no longer flies, but it is not completely switched off: NASA set it up to keep waking up and storing data like a small test station, waiting for someone to collect them one day.
ingenuity.fun: Ingenuity carries a tiny piece of fabric from the Wright brothers' Flyer, the first powered airplane on Earth. Two first flights, connected across more than a century.

deposito-three-forks.name: Three Forks sample depot
deposito-three-forks.story: Not everything left in space is abandoned: some things are stored. Between December 2022 and January 2023, the Perseverance rover carefully dropped ten metal tubes onto the floor of Jezero Crater, at a place called Three Forks. Inside are pieces of rock, Martian dust and even a sample of the air. It is a kind of backup safe for the future.
deposito-three-forks.science: Billions of years ago, Jezero was a lake with a river delta. On Earth, rocks like these keep traces of ancient life. Analyzing them in laboratories on Earth, with equipment impossible to take to Mars, could answer the big question: was there ever life on Mars?
deposito-three-forks.today: The tubes are still laid out on the ground in a zigzag pattern so they are easy to find. How and when to bring them to Earth is still being discussed.
deposito-three-forks.fun: One of the tubes is a “witness tube”: it has no rock in it, but it shows whether the others could have been contaminated with material carried from Earth.

maven.name: MAVEN
maven.story: Long ago, Mars had thicker air and perhaps rivers and lakes. Today it is a cold desert with a very thin atmosphere. MAVEN arrived in 2014 to solve the mystery: where did that air go? For eleven years it circled the planet measuring the gases escaping into space. In December 2025 it stopped communicating and, after months of attempts, NASA declared the mission over in 2026.
maven.science: MAVEN discovered that the solar wind, a stream of particles coming from the Sun, slowly strips away the atmosphere of Mars, especially during solar storms. Because Mars lost its protective magnetic field, it was left exposed. MAVEN also worked as a relay antenna, sending messages from the rovers to Earth.
maven.today: MAVEN is still circling Mars, but silently. Its farewell left fewer spacecraft watching the planet, which already has an aging fleet.
maven.fun: MAVEN carried a DVD with more than a thousand haikus about Mars, written and voted on by the public from all over the world.

voyager-1.name: Voyager 1
voyager-1.story: Voyager 1 is the human-made object that has traveled the farthest. It was launched in 1977, visited Jupiter and Saturn, and in 2012 left the bubble the Sun creates around itself to enter interstellar space. Its signals take almost a full day to reach Earth. To save power, the team has been switching off its instruments one by one: today only two are still on.
voyager-1.science: Voyager 1 discovered active volcanoes on Io, one of Jupiter's moons, and studied the atmosphere of Titan, Saturn's large moon. Now it measures particles and magnetic fields in a region no other spacecraft had reached. It runs on a nuclear generator that loses about 4 watts of power every year.
voyager-1.today: It is still alive almost 49 years after launch. Every instrument switched off stretches its life a little longer. One day its signal will stop arriving, but the spacecraft will keep traveling among the stars.
voyager-1.fun: In 1990 it turned its camera and photographed Earth from 6 billion km away: a “pale blue dot”. It also carries a golden record with greetings in 55 languages, music and sounds of our planet.

voyager-2.name: Voyager 2
voyager-2.story: Voyager 2 lifted off two weeks before its twin, but on a longer route. It took advantage of a planetary alignment that happens every 175 years to hop from one planet to the next like a relay race. It passed Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. To this day, it is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune. In 2018 it also crossed the border into interstellar space.
voyager-2.science: It used each planet's gravity like a slingshot to gain speed and change course, a technique called gravity assist. It discovered new moons and rings around Uranus and Neptune, and photographed a great dark spot on Neptune, a giant storm.
voyager-2.today: Like Voyager 1, it is still sending data with very few instruments switched on, because its power is slowly running out. The team carefully decides what to switch off so it lasts as long as possible.
voyager-2.fun: It carries the same golden record as Voyager 1. On it are the sounds of rain, a heartbeat and a mother talking to her baby.

pioneer-10.name: Pioneer 10
pioneer-10.story: Pioneer 10 was the explorer that led the way. Nobody knew whether a spacecraft could cross the asteroid belt without being destroyed. Pioneer 10 made it through safe and sound and, in 1973, became the first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter. It kept moving away and sending signals for almost 31 years, until in 2003 its power was no longer enough to talk to Earth.
pioneer-10.science: It measured for the first time the intense radiation surrounding Jupiter, much stronger than expected. That information was vital to protect the spacecraft that came later, like the Voyagers. It also took the first close-up images of the giant planet.
pioneer-10.today: It is still traveling silently toward the constellation Taurus. It will take about two million years to pass near the star Aldebaran.
pioneer-10.fun: It carries a metal plaque with a drawing of two people and a map showing where the Sun is, in case someone finds it one day.

new-horizons.name: New Horizons
new-horizons.story: When New Horizons lifted off in 2006, Pluto was a blurry smudge in telescopes. It traveled nine and a half years to get there. On July 14, 2015 it flew past Pluto and showed us an incredible world, with mountains of ice and a big white “heart”. Then it went on to Arrokoth, an icy rock shaped like a snowman, the most distant object ever explored up close.
new-horizons.science: It discovered that Pluto has slowly flowing nitrogen glaciers, mountains of water ice and a bluish atmosphere. Arrokoth showed how the first building blocks that formed the planets came together, more than 4.5 billion years ago.
new-horizons.today: It is still active, traveling through the Kuiper Belt and studying the dust and particles of that distant region of the solar system.
new-horizons.fun: It carries a small portion of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto in 1930.
